To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the solid CO2:CO2 abundance ratio is ~1:3 in quiescent clouds and increases to ~1:1 in low-mass envelopes; (2) the solid CO:CO2 abundance is ~1:4 in quiescent regions and decreases to ~1:20 in low-mass star-forming regions; (3) the solid CO and CO2 abundances in low-mass cores are higher than those in quiescent gas, but are lower

the solid CO2 abundance is higher in low-mass than in high-mass star-forming regions; that the solid CO abundance is higher in high-mass than in low-mass star-formng regions; that solid CO is a major constituent of the ice in the inner envelope around low-mass protosars; that the CO2 ice in the inner regions around low-mass starforming protostars is pure and crystalline; that the solid H2O abundance is higher in the inner

the solid CO2 ice abundance in low-mass star forming regions is high relative to water and CO, and that the CO2 ice profile is best explained as a superposition of two distinct components, one of which is found to be CO2:H2 O rich.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of ices in the inner envelopes of low-mass young stars, and the formation and evolution of the CO and CO2 ice bands.
the evolution of ices around embedded low-mass protobinaries.
the evolution of solid CO2 in the inner regions (< 100 AU) of low-mass protoplanetary disks, where the ice is likely to be the dominant reservoir of carbon in the early stages of planet formation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the CO2 bending band profile is the result of a combination of thermal and chemical processing of CO2 and CO ices in the inner regions (<100 AU) of low-mass protosolar nebulae.
the formation of pure crystalline CO2 is a multi-step process involving both distillation and segregation.

the solid CO2:CO and CO2:H20 components are formed in the low-density and high-density environments respectively and the subsequent evolution of these components are caused by distillation due to thermal processing.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the CO2:water and CO2:CO components are formed in different environments, with the CO2: CO component being formed in the higher density regions of molecular cloud cores and the CO2:H_2O component being formed in lower density regions.

CO2 ice is formed early on in the star-forming process in the low-density, quiescent environment of a molecular cloud, and then evolves with the protostar as a result of distillation of the ice due to thermal processing.

CO2 ice is a ubiquitous component of the solid material in the inner regions (within a few hundred AU) of the circumstellar envelopes of embedded low-mass protosolar systems, with an average abundance relative to water that is 1.5 times higher than that found around massive protostellar objects.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the formation of CO2 in the ice mantles around low-mass protosolars is likely a complex process involving both low-temperature freeze-out of CO2 in low-density environments and high temperature distillation from CO in dense, high temperature regions.

the solid-state chemistry of CO2 is more complex than previously thought and that the formation of pure, crystalline solid CO2 may not occur until after the CO2:H 2O ice has been completely evaporated.

CO2:CO and CO2:H20 are distinct components that form in distinct physical conditions, and that CO2 is a key component of the chemical inventory of the inner envelope of low-mass protosolar systems, where it can survive the thermal processing of the envelope.
